newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn sets full Lufthansa privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Bonn sets full Lufthansa privatisation.

text.p: Germany's Transport Ministry said on Tuesday it had agreed draft laws that would permit full privatisation of Deutsche Lufthansa AG by introducing steps to ensure a majority of the airline would remain in German hands.
"I am confident that, with the help of this law, the (remaining state-owned stake) can be floated this year," German Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann said in a statement.
The German government currently holds a 36 percent stake in Frankfurt-quoted Lufthansa. At present market levels, that shareholding is worth some three billion marks ($1.9 billion).
Matthias said the new law would mean that all future stock issued in German airline businesses would be registered shares that were not freely transferable.
The Ministry said that from this March, a computer-based trading system would be available for such shares that would allow them to be traded "as easily and reliably as ordinary shares".

A shareholding book would then allow an airline to assess its shareholding structure by nationality. Airlines need to retain a majority of domestic ownership to meet national air sector agreements in most countries.

If more than 40 percent of its shares fell into foreign hands, the airline would then be allowed to buy back its own stock. If the proportion rose above 45 percent, a new share issue in which existing shareholders would not be allowed to take part would be possible.
In the extreme case that foreign shareholders gained more than 50 percent of an airline's shares, the company would be permitted to force foreign shareholders to sell their stock.
At present, Lufthansa is the only company to which the new law will apply. At the moment, foreign investors hold some 20 percent.
A Lufthansa spokesman said in response to enquiries that the company expected that under such a law, existing shares would have to be converted into non-freely transferable shares.
